fields.expected: I'd want to work on infrastructure for scientific research, specifically the evaluation side of it. Over the past year I studied independently how research gets funded and selected, reading history from patronage through Bell Labs to the NIH project-grant model and newer structures like DARPA, ARPA-H, and Focused Research Organizations, and talking with researchers, administrators, economists, and people building alternative research institutions. I started out convinced that grant-writing time was the main constraint on science. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and the illegible ones never get attempted. What pulled me toward building rather than just reading is the current asymmetry. AI is making generation cheap, including literature search, analysis, and testing alternative specifications, while judgment stays expensive because reviewers have limited time and domain expertise doesn't scale. I got interested in this concretely at Intelehealth, where I built an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard and found that producing an answer was trivial next to deciding whether to trust it. So: a company building methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, reproducibility, and evidence tracing for AI-generated technical work, with real escalation paths to human experts.

fields.expected: The hardest has been the machine-learning core of the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system I work on at Summer Atlantic Capital. I own large parts of the data and ML infrastructure, including the event-ingestion pipeline, the versioned FastAPI microservice, the public detection API, and the repository and CI scaffold, plus temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN and Transformer-style approaches. The modeling itself was hard, but the harder problem turned out to be that a technically good detector can still be useless. An anomaly system that fires too often just replaces the original problem with a triage problem, and analysts stop reading the alerts. That pushed me into work I didn't expect to be doing: a learning-to-rank layer for prioritizing alerts rather than only scoring them, and a retrieval-augmented LLM explanation layer so an analyst can see why something was flagged instead of receiving a score with no context. I had to get much more careful about what I was actually optimizing, since offline detection metrics don't tell you whether the output changes what a human does. Failure modes, explanation quality, and documentation ended up mattering as much as the model architecture.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was on campus. We followed him to Garland Hall, found the doors locked, saw him through the glass, and knocked until someone let us in long enough to pitch him on what we were building. It was awkward and we were clearly not on anyone's schedule. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it less because of the outcome and more because it corrected something I believed. I had assumed that if the technical work was good enough, the right people would eventually notice. They don't. Recruiting users, explaining repeatedly why a thing should exist, and putting yourself in rooms you weren't invited to are a real part of making something exist, not overhead around the engineering. I'm not naturally comfortable doing that, which is part of why knocking on that door mattered to me.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer resonates more. The work I've found most useful has always involved a specific user operating under constraints I couldn't understand from a spec. At Intelehealth I worked on AI and data systems for rural telemedicine, and one project was a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages that combined facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps data, weather, and healthcare-resource availability. None of the hard parts were the code. The hard parts were deciding what counted as a reachable facility, how to handle missing data honestly, and what a clinician actually needed to see to make a decision. I also built the evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs there, using stratified sampling over a 4,169-case benchmark to surface systematic failure modes rather than reporting a single accuracy number, because the deployment context determined which errors mattered. I like moving between implementation and the institutional question of how the output gets used, and I'd rather work where there is a concrete user and a real failure mode than build against an abstract requirement. I'd still want to write substantial infrastructure, not just configure things, which is what appeals to me about the FDSE role specifically.
